negatives.text: Paint on the upper sections of both lifeboats had faded, with no maintenance planned.
Weekly and monthly lifeboat checks had been completed without noting the discoloration.
HVPQ photo 6 (transom from astern) was too dark to show the condition clearly.

crew: Junior deck officer completed LSA checks without noting faded lifeboat paint
stories.headline: Faded lifeboats and a photo too dark to judge
stories.dek: Three minor observations: lifeboat paint faded without a maintenance plan, routine checks that missed it, and an HVPQ photo too dark to use.
takeaways: Note cosmetic LSA issues such as faded lifeboat paint in weekly checks and plan the repaint.
Check every HVPQ photo is bright, clear and shows the required view before upload.
An all-ticked LSA checklist next to a visible defect counts against you; write down what you see.

positives.text: Walked through planned enclosed space entries for upcoming tank squeezing: detailed RAs, crew training records, pre-job meeting and office approvals.

crew: Senior deck officer was credited for preparing upcoming tank entries well in advance
stories.headline: Nil observations and a positive for enclosed space planning
stories.dek: A clean SIRE 2.0 result with no negative observations, and the senior deck officer credited for planning upcoming enclosed space entries in detail.
takeaways: Plan enclosed space entries for upcoming jobs early: RA, permit, rescue kit and office approval ready before the inspector asks.
Keep the crew training records for the job on file and be ready to show them with the risk assessment.
Hold and record a pre-job meeting before any tank entry and be able to explain what was discussed.

stories.style: Rated easy-going. Practical and professional, but interviewed every officer and rating alone: no senior officer or office staff was allowed in the room during interviews.
gaps: Flagged by inspector, not recorded: ECDIS keyboard and mouse did not match the maker's type-approval certificate.
Fixed gas detection was isolated for all ballast tanks during a part discharge, even tanks not being ballasted.
Officers needed training on the purpose and use of the fixed gas detection system.
condition: Deck hydraulic lines and their valves heavily corroded.
Inert gas fresh-air intake flange found open while the IG system was in use.
Warping drum paint not removed, although reported as closed out.
Lifebuoy grab lines frayed; lifeboat fall turnbuckles dry and corroded; boat's reflective tape poor.
Vapour line marked only on the reducer, not along the line; paint store water spray labelled as sprinklers.
Forward winch gear oil milky and the level hard to read in the sight glass.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: emergency generator room door seal had hardened.
PV breaker flame screen rusting; light outside the pumproom entrance not working.
crew: Officers answered satisfactorily but sometimes needed help to show where the SMS covered a topic.
Flagged by inspector: ETO was slow to reset the emergency generator fuel tank quick-closing valve.
Flagged by inspector: a crew member did not know how many wheeled extinguishers were in the engine room.
stories.headline: Singapore: one-to-one interviews, no seniors in the room
stories.dek: A friendly but firm inspector interviewed each crew member alone; the walk-round found heavy hydraulic corrosion, an open IG fresh-air flange and isolated gas detection.
takeaways: Prepare every crew member to answer alone; seniors and office staff may be kept out of interviews.
Blank the IG fresh-air intake whenever the inert gas system is in use.
Know when fixed gas detection points may be isolated, and isolate only what the operation needs.

negatives.text: The radar maintenance procedure was not aligned with the maker's operation manual, except for magnetron replacement.
Company required the incinerator risk assessment to be reviewed and recorded before each use; garbage records showed a recent incineration with no review recorded.
Bonding straps on a bunker fuel transfer line next to a cargo tank had moderate rust; already noted in the safety inspection and planned after discharge.

stories.headline: Malta OPL: three findings, one already on the job list
stories.dek: Radar maintenance that did not match the maker's manual, an unreviewed incinerator risk assessment, and rusty bonding straps already scheduled for repair.
takeaways: Align radar maintenance routines with the maker's manual, not just magnetron changes.
If the SMS says to review a risk assessment before each use, record that review every time.
A defect already on your own list can still be an observation; fix visible ones before arrival where possible.

stories.style: Rated easy-going. Practical and unhurried; asked crew only a few basic questions. Focused on LSA/FFA and on equipment he expected to suffer early material failure. Reduced most of his observations himself on risk grounds.

questions.q: What is an enclosed space?
What is a risk assessment? Are you ever involved, and how do you contribute?
What is a near miss?
What would you do if you saw someone working unsafely?

gaps: Five months after joining the fleet, there was no working PMS for most key machinery and no interim paper system.
Crew needed training in record keeping after the management change.
No inspection records for the mast riser duct.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: engineers' call alarm tested only in cabins and the ECR, not in common areas.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: no company safety instructions on lathe workpiece length and use of supports.
condition: Two PV valves leaking gas.
Generator quick-closing valves lashed with wire.
A portable pneumatic pump used to remove oil leaking from a generator.
Manifold blanks secured with bolts showing fewer than two threads.
Warping drum and bitter end painted; winch brake pointers not set correctly.
Hydraulic oil leaks at the windlass brakes, deck valve control boxes and forepeak store motors.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: lifeboat auto-release gripe wires badly corroded.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: deck lights and a store torch were not intrinsically safe.
crew: Officers and crew satisfactory but needed support at times so answers did not become observations.
stories.headline: Antifer: a takeover ship with no working PMS
stories.dek: An easy-going inspector asked the crew four simple questions; the real exposure was a ship five months into new management without a working maintenance system.
takeaways: After a management change, run an interim PMS on paper or spreadsheet until the software is ready.
Every rating should explain enclosed spaces, their role in risk assessment, near misses and stopping unsafe work.
Never lash quick-closing valves; they must operate freely.

stories.style: Rated easy-going. Practical and professional; praised the engine room's appearance and the crew's effort, asked basic questions and was patient, prompting officers when they hesitated.
gaps: Flagged by inspector, not recorded: parallel index lines were taken off buoys and drying heights instead of fixed references.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: ENC not marked where safety settings should be changed.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: last test date of the paint store water spray system not stencilled outside the space.
Ship exceeded its cross-track limit on approach with no bell book entry or passage plan amendment.
Cargo and bunker overfill alarms could not run together, yet no notice barred loading and bunkering at once.
Fire alarm test records had not been kept since the management change; no PMS records for the N2 plant.
No echo sounder comparison records against the hand lead line; spare cargo hoses not in the PMS.
condition: Mooring winches needed urgent attention: hydraulic flanges badly rusted, control box nuts corroded.
Fire wire rigged with one turn on the first bollard instead of two turns and a figure of eight.
Warping drums still painted and bitter end painted over instead of clean and greased.
Mooring lines not tight to their markings or tended properly; forward springs showed compression damage.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: large gap between the lifeboat traverse plate and the boat body.
Pumproom rescue hatch had no fixed guide wire for the stretcher; rescue rope not fire retardant.
Crankcase doors not marked as enclosed spaces; engine room exit signs and IMO symbols missing or misplaced.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: a ballast tank overflowed during the inspection because of an erratic gauge.
crew: Officers answered the inspector's questions but often needed help to find where the SMS covered a topic.
Flagged by inspector: the OOW did not know the procedure for crossing the safety contour.
stories.headline: Easy-going in Sohar, but the mooring deck told its own story
stories.dek: A patient inspector praised the engine room and prompted the officers; the consultant still listed 31 points, many on winches, line handling and markings.
takeaways: Rig fire wires with two turns on the first bollard and a figure of eight, and keep mooring lines tended.
Remove paint from warping drums and grease bitter ends so they work in an emergency.
Mark where ENC safety settings change, and know the procedure before crossing the safety contour.

stories.style: Rated normal. Experienced and practical; stayed on board overnight across two days. Mostly kept to the tablet, dug deep only where he suspected a safety issue, and recorded obvious findings. Briefly lost his temper over sharing a toilet overnight.
gaps: No procedure in the SMS or cargo manuals to make sure high level alarms stay functional.
No procedure to review the UKC calculation with the pilot during the Master-pilot exchange.
SIMOPS decision matrix not available in the engine control room.
Fire detection system gave repeated alarms that ship staff could not trace.
Terminal rules prevented testing of overfill alarms, lifeboat engine, emergency generator and fire pump.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: poor crew responses and overall deck maintenance.
condition: Scuppers not tight enough to stop an oil leak; several tank dome butterfly bolts not even hand tight.
Steam return line flange leaking; main steam isolation valves not holding.
Pumproom steam line lagging detached; water leaking near the BWTS UV reactor.
SART telescopic pole did not fit the SARTs carried; crew unsure how to mount them in survival craft.
Winch brake marks out of line while moored with brakes fully on; anchor swivels worn.
Deck pad eyes without SWL; several deck markings faded or written in marker pen.
VDR showing an input failure alarm; vapour return pressure gauge read zero with pumps running.
Anti-splash tape missing on an auxiliary engine control airline.
crew: C/O and 2/O were well prepared and presented well; the Master was involved everywhere.
3/O, on a first contract in rank, lacked confidence.
C/E said little and lacked confidence; 2/E was hard-working but struggled under questioning.
3/E explained the N2 generator well; an AB excelled on enclosed space entry and gangway rigging.
4/E did not know how many wheeled extinguishers were in the engine room; an Oiler managed SCBA checks.
stories.headline: Amsterdam overnight: loose scuppers and a nervous engine room
stories.dek: A fair inspector spent nine hours over two days; deck officers shone, but senior engineers struggled and loose fittings on deck drew attention.
takeaways: Check scuppers and tank dome bolts are tight before arrival.
Confirm SART poles actually fit the SARTs on board, and practise mounting them.
Trace and fix nuisance fire alarms before the inspection.

negatives.text: Junior deck officer did not understand the ECDIS date-dependent function and wrongly said date-dependent information could be marked on the chart by hand.
Procedures did not cover AIS use while discharging hydrocarbons (switch off, isolate the aerial or use a dummy load, per ISGOTT); the ship was discharging at the time.
No meter able to measure CO2 as required by IMO MSC.581(110) was on board; one had been ordered and was awaited.
The emergency towing light on the poop deck did not work.
Senior deck officer thought the towing light only worked in darkness; tested in the dark it still failed, working only with its cover loosened, suggesting a loose connection.

positives.text: Showed correct lifejacket donning and the pre-use checks, including the light, whistle and overall condition of the jacket.

crew: Junior deck officer was unfamiliar with the ECDIS date-dependent display
Senior deck officer misjudged the emergency towing light defect
Rating earned a positive for lifejacket checks
stories.headline: ECDIS date-dependent gap and a dead emergency towing light
stories.dek: Five observations, from ECDIS knowledge and AIS use during discharge to a missing CO2 meter and a faulty towing light, with one rating positive.
takeaways: Learn how ECDIS shows date-dependent objects and how to set the viewing date for the voyage.
Know what your procedure says about AIS during cargo operations; ISGOTT expects it off, isolated or on a dummy load.
Test emergency lights in darkness or by covering the sensor, and fix faults before arrival.

stories.style: Rated normal. Experienced, practical and fair. Stuck to the tablet questions with some cross-questioning, went deep only in a few areas, recorded only the obvious findings and let many minor points pass. Calm and approachable.
gaps: Bunker line draining procedure was missing from the SMS.
SMS did not state clearly what records to keep for cargo loading, discharging and ballast operations.
No time log was kept for the bunkering operation.
No electrical failure response plan was available.
Bunker line pressure relief valve test procedure was unclear.
PV valve settings on the CCR poster did not match the values stencilled on the valves.
MSDS file had no index, and there was no inspection record for the N2 buffer tank.
condition: Flagged by inspector, not recorded: corrosion along the deck steam line.
Corrosion setting in along the catwalk; spot rust on deck frames, flanges and pipes.
Provision crane hook had a loosely fitted spring lock plate.
Forward emergency towing chain box was covered and lashed, so not ready for use in port.
One portable multigas meter was not working.
Engine room bottom-platform gratings not clamped; raised-edge mats at switchboards were trip hazards.
Bridge wing fire line gauge was opaque; pyrotechnics were not in waterproof bags.
Two-way radios had no operating instructions; HF/MF aerials had green deposits.
crew: Overall satisfactory, though a few crew members were below expectation.
Crew could not say where the emergency towing booklet was kept.
stories.headline: Rouen: a steady inspector who logged only the obvious
stories.dek: A practical, tablet-focused inspector recorded only clear-cut issues, while the consultant's walk-round found corroded steam lines, loose records and trip hazards.
takeaways: Make sure PV valve settings posted in the CCR match what is stencilled on the valves.
Keep a time log for every bunkering and have a written bunker line draining procedure.
Keep the emergency towing gear ready in port and know where the towing booklet is.

stories.style: Rated normal. Senior; said at the start there would be no negotiation. Patient and professional, prompted crew but let no one else answer. Adapted calmly when cargo operations changed order; removed a few points fixed on the spot, then no more.
gaps: C/O showed procedures from an outdated downloaded copy of the SMS instead of the current revision.
Main deck safety officer inspections exceeded the company's 3-monthly interval.
No complete lock-out/tag-out kit on board.
Emergency generator instructions unclear on putting it on load manually if it does not connect itself.
No record that pitch control from the emergency control position had been tested.
Accommodation doors locked from inside at security level 1.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: fire pump starting procedure missing.
condition: Steam lines in very poor condition along the full length of the deck despite a recent dry dock.
Helideck plates, deck gratings and steps badly corroded or broken.
Hydraulic leak on deck being caught in a bucket placed underneath.
Soft mooring ropes in poor condition, no chafing guards, warping drum painted, locking pins not in place.
Studs missing from ballast tank manholes; tank cleaning line valve handwheels missing.
Emergency steering gear room blower not working and the room very hot.
Main engine high-pressure fuel lines without anti-splash tape; under-piston doors not marked as enclosed spaces.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: bonding wires broken on fuel and other lines; an engine room emergency light not working.
crew: Most officers and ratings satisfactory; the 2/O was sharp and hard-working.
C/O and 3/O did not answer basic questions to SIRE 2.0 standard.
Flagged by inspector: 3/O could not engage the lifeboat lever to run it ahead and astern.
stories.headline: Suape: no negotiation, and steam lines that couldn't hide
stories.dek: A patient but firm inspector ruled out bargaining from the start; the consultant's list ran past 30 items, led by badly corroded steam lines and helideck plates.
takeaways: Always show procedures from the current SMS revision, not a downloaded copy.
Keep safety officer inspections within the company interval; inspectors check the dates.
Make sure every officer can operate lifeboat controls, including ahead and astern.

stories.style: Rated tough. Senior and demanding; set expectations at the opening meeting. Sometimes aggressive in interviews and visibly agitated by poor answers, though he gave hints. Wanted simple, practical answers and to see the SMS procedure behind almost everything.

questions.q: Show enclosed space entry permits and explain the procedure.
When was the lifeboat last lowered to the water, and where is that recorded?
Show the enhanced survey (ESP) file and the audits declared in the PIQ.
Show the Master's navigation audit and behaviour-based safety records.
Show BNWAS, Aldis lamp and EPIRB test records.
How is the ECDIS maintained, and where is that job in the PMS?
Walk through the current passage plan.
What voluntary security reporting scheme applies in this area?
On the deck round, explain rescue boat and freefall lifeboat checks.
How is the double hull space inerted?
What are the retirement criteria for mooring ropes?
Show gas meter testing and calibration records.
What is the procedure for sampling toxic cargo?
Demonstrate donning and checking an SCBA.
Show PMS jobs and critical spares; explain the hot work procedure.

gaps: ECDIS maintenance jobs were not in the PMS.
Maintenance of several pieces of equipment not in the PMS, risking missed routines.
Security risk assessment not in the passage plan; access control and evacuation security drills not done per the SSP.
Magnetron renewal not updated in the PMS records.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: weekly and monthly LSA/FFA maintenance not entered in the deck log as the PMS requires.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: no PMS job or maintenance record for pipeline bonding cables.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: emergency generator spring starter not charged and ready to start.
condition: Holes in the athwartships main steam line on deck; main steam line heavily corroded.
Engine room sea water overboard pipe leaking, with a temporary repair in place.
Aft spring winch hydraulic block leaking; spring winch brake bands corroded and pitted.
Port upper deck door would not close fully because of a deformed frame.
Ballast water treatment system out of service on a deferred defect.
440 V insulation monitor alarm set at 2 megohms against an expected 5 megohms.
Scrubber module alarm, a gas detection flow fault and a ballast tank gauge with no readout.
One foam monitor valve leaking; spare on order.
crew: Officers and crew average overall; SMS knowledge and filing satisfactory.
2/O performed well below average and was reluctant to act on advice.
stories.headline: Nine hours under pressure: a tough inspector who wants it in the SMS
stories.dek: A demanding senior inspector questioned hard, sometimes aggressively, and asked to see the written company procedure behind almost every answer.
takeaways: For every routine you describe, be ready to open the SMS page that requires it.
Put ECDIS maintenance, bonding cable checks and every critical item into the PMS.
Keep the emergency generator ready to start, including a charged spring starter.

stories.style: Rated normal. Experienced, practical and fair; the inspection was spread over two days. Stuck to the tablet with some cross-questioning, went deep only in certain areas, recorded the obvious and let many minor points pass. Calm and approachable.
gaps: Inspector showed an expired ID at the gangway and the gangway watch did not check it.
No visitors' list at the gangway.
Safety checklist completed on the computer instead of by hand.
Company guidance on behavioural competency assessment did not set out what the assessor should look for.
A change of ECDIS safety settings from coastal to restricted waters was not logged.
Paint room fixed fire-fighting procedure did not include closing the drain valve.
condition: At least three poop deck scuppers came loose when the inspector tapped them with his foot.
Chain locker and deck crane post not marked as enclosed spaces; pumproom emergency bilge suction unmarked.
Forward emergency towing chain box covered and lashed; aft towing wire drum cover still on.
Lifeboat launching instructions unreadable due to rust stains; pyrotechnics not in waterproof bags.
A cargo pump tripped unexpectedly during the visit; root cause still under investigation.
Hydraulic valve boxes on deck corroding at the butterfly bolts.
crew: Pumpman was praised by the inspector; the Bosun answered well on DPA contact details.
Gangway AB answered well and handled it correctly once the inspector's expired ID was pointed out.
C/O crossed a mooring rope under tension in front of the inspector.
Deck watchkeeper could not explain pilot ladder rigging; 4/E could not explain hazardous energy well.
stories.headline: The expired ID at the gangway that nobody checked
stories.dek: Over two days, a fair inspector noted the obvious; a missed ID check, a C/O crossing a taut mooring line and loose scuppers stood out.
takeaways: Check every visitor's ID properly at the gangway, the inspector's included, and keep a visitors' list.
Never step over or near mooring lines under tension, least of all with an inspector watching.
Mark chain lockers, crane posts and similar spaces as enclosed spaces.

stories.style: Rated tough. Experienced but argumentative; started from the tablet then investigated beyond it, cross-questioned heavily and dug for non-obvious findings, especially in documents. Became uneasy when challenged.
gaps: Rest hour records showed several rest periods under 1 hour, yet the rest hours software raised no non-conformity.
Familiarisation checklist had no job-specific sections for ETO, Pumpman, Cook and messman.
Distress, urgency and safety DSC messages not recorded in the GMDSS log; weekly and monthly tests mixed up.
Cargo entered under its commercial name in the Oil Record Book Part II.
No allowance for winch brake lining wear; brake settings unchanged after heavy use.
No procedure or key for manual release of the water mist system if its solenoid valve fails.
Three hard copies of COSWP not available, only electronic copies.
condition: A stud in the anchor chain not welded at one end; chain looked thinned down.
Blower trunk door frame badly corroded and painted over; a mist catcher vane damaged.
Oil spray at the starboard manifold not cleaned; a blow line cap missing.
Emergency towing chain box covered and lashed, so not ready for use in port.
Gangway angle over 30 degrees.
Bridge wing RPM indicator and repeater not working; bridge door lock broken; server room unlocked.
Boiler chemical dosing tank lid missing with no PPE nearby; oily rag drum almost full.
Forward liferaft painter secured to a fixed point; fire doors had open screw holes.
crew: Overall performance satisfactory, but only just manageable.
A crew member could not name the two main hazards of nitrogen.
Officers were unclear on the radar performance test and the double block and bleed valve.
Some crew did not know the galley wet chemical extinguisher's electrical rating or to set radios to low power.
stories.headline: Antwerp: an inspector who investigated instead of inspecting
stories.dek: An argumentative senior inspector left the tablet to dig for hidden findings, especially in records, from rest hours to the GMDSS log.
takeaways: Check rest hour records for rest periods under one hour and raise the non-conformity yourself.
Log every DSC distress, urgency and safety message received in the GMDSS log.
Make sure crew can name the hazards of nitrogen and explain double block and bleed valves.

negatives.text: Junior deck officer could not explain the response to a cargo leak into a double hull space, or where the hose connection for inerting that space was kept.
Gas meters on board covered O2, CO, H2S and HC/LEL, but none could measure CO2 as now required by IMO MSC.581(110).
Enclosed space entry procedures and checklist did not yet include CO2 testing in line with MSC.581(110).

positives.text: Explained a recent enclosed space entry in depth: risk assessment, toolbox meeting, rescue equipment ready and permit validity.
Explained the SIMOPS procedure and matrix with enthusiasm, including his own duties and several scenarios.
Described rigging and recovering the accommodation ladder, including toolbox talk, risk assessment and required PPE.

crew: Ratings earned three positives for enclosed space entry, SIMOPS and ladder rigging
Junior deck officer was unsure of the double hull cargo leak response
stories.headline: Ratings earn three positives, CO2 gas testing catches the ship out
stories.dek: Three observations, two on the new IMO requirement to test for CO2 before enclosed space entry, and three positives for confident, well-briefed ratings.
takeaways: Check you carry a meter that measures CO2 and that your entry checklist includes it (MSC.581(110)).
Officers should know the double hull cargo leak plan and where the inerting connection is stowed.
Brief ratings on SIMOPS: their role, the matrix and example scenarios.

stories.style: Rated normal. Practical and unhurried; worked through the standard questions without questioning crew much. Would not remove a recorded observation but agreed to amend its wording on request.
gaps: Enclosed space permit did not include a CO2 check, although a CO2-capable meter was on board.
Safety officer checklist findings had no target date or actual close-out date.
Breath alcohol tester inherited from the previous managers was past its calibration interval.
Crew new to the company needed training in record keeping.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: 3/O marked a list of about 20 rig warnings as off-route without checking each one.
crew: 3/O needed too much hand-holding for a takeover ship doing STS operations.
C/E was new to the company and still learning the SMS.
C/O was new and not taking rest when he could, risking fatigue.
stories.headline: Offshore STS: a takeover ship still learning its new SMS
stories.dek: At an offshore STS area a practical inspector kept to standard questions; the bigger worry was a new crew still learning company systems and a tired C/O.
takeaways: Check every navigational warning against your route individually; never dismiss a list in bulk.
If a CO2 meter is on board, make the CO2 reading part of the enclosed space permit.
Senior officers should take rest when they can, especially on STS ships.

negatives.text: The latest cargo pump hydraulic oil analysis was normal, but the previous report had flagged high particle counts.

stories.headline: One observation: an earlier oil analysis warning
stories.dek: A near-clean SIRE 2.0 with a single hardware observation: an earlier hydraulic oil analysis showing high particle counts in the cargo pump system.
takeaways: Act on every abnormal oil analysis result and record the follow-up, even if the next sample is fine.
Inspectors read past analysis reports, not just the latest; keep the trend and actions together.
Include cargo pump hydraulic oil in the analysis programme and review its trend before an inspection.

stories.style: Rated easy-going by the attending consultant. A senior, practical inspector with strong chemical tanker knowledge who prompted answers to put crew at ease, and taught basics on the spot instead of writing them up.
gaps: Enclosed space permit did not include a CO2 check, and no instrument able to measure CO2 was on board.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: cargo polymerisation contingency checklist had no step to save VDR data.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: GMDSS station was not switched off during bunkering.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: GMDSS pre-departure checks were not carried out as required.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: Master-pilot exchange did not cover ECDIS details as NP232 expects.
condition: Deck steam line near the manifold needed cosmetic work.
Starboard lifeboat winch leaking oil; port lifeboat painter frayed and damaged in places.
Port gangway handrail ropes badly frayed.
Spare fire extinguishers had not been inspected for several months.
One portable multigas meter's battery would not charge.
ECDIS mouse and keyboard were not on the maker's approved hardware list.
No record that the ECDIS hard drive was renewed at dry dock, as the maker advises every 5 years.
Electrical receptacle boxes on the bridge wing and at the manifold could not be opened easily.
crew: Crew knew the SMS well and answered confidently.
Bosun singled out as especially hard-working.
stories.headline: A teaching inspector who coached crew instead of writing them up
stories.dek: A senior, chemical-savvy inspector prompted and coached the crew, while the consultant still found frayed ropes, ECDIS hardware gaps and no CO2 checks.
takeaways: Add a CO2 reading to the enclosed space permit and make sure a CO2-capable meter is on board.
Check ECDIS mouse and keyboard against the maker's approved list and keep hard drive renewal records.
Isolate the GMDSS MF/HF station during bunkering, as the safety checklist expects.

stories.style: Rated tough. Treated every question like an investigation, cross-checking each answer with another crew member or a certificate and spending long on each item. Quick to call a negative, and read the questions his own way.

questions.q: What is the purpose of parallel indexing on the radar?
Does the procedure require reducing speed while the pilot or combination ladder is rigged?
Match each lifting appliance in the inventory to its certificate number.
Was the visiting border official given a safety familiarisation at the gangway?

gaps: Enclosed space permit did not include a CO2 check, and no CO2-capable meter was supplied.
Latest SMS revision (new SIMOPS matrix) had not reached the ship's SMS software or been sent by email.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: lifting equipment inventory lacked details SIRE expects; items could not be matched to certificates.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: no procedure on reducing speed while rigging the pilot or combination ladder.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: visiting border officials were not given a safety familiarisation at the gangway.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: 2/O's rest hour record showed rest while the ship was mooring.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: a past pumproom drill record carried signatures that did not match the Master on board then.
condition: Bunker line valves outside the pumproom not marked with the tanks they serve.
Main steam line valve from the engine room leaking; soft patch on a ballast line in the pumproom.
Overspeed trip buttons on all three cargo pumps not labelled.
ECDIS mouse and keyboard not on the approved hardware list; no record of hard drive renewal.
Generator top bolt covers cracked or missing; a portable gas meter showed a flow fault.
Forward breast lines damaged and due for replacement.
Intrinsically safe light outside the pumproom showing internal corrosion.
A dairy item from the provision supplier had no expiry date.
crew: Crew knew the SMS well and answered confidently.
Bosun and Pumpman stood out as hard-working.
Flagged by inspector: 2/O was unsure why parallel indexing is used on radar.
stories.headline: Baytown: an inspector who audited like an investigator
stories.dek: Every answer was cross-checked with a second crew member or a certificate, turning the inspection into a long, adversarial day.
takeaways: Expect answers to be verified: have the record, certificate and the person who did the job ready.
Make rest hour records reflect reality, especially around mooring and cargo stations.
Give every visitor, officials included, a safety familiarisation at the gangway and record it.

stories.style: Rated normal. Practical and unhurried; worked through the standard questions without questioning crew much. Would not remove a recorded observation but agreed to amend its wording on request.
gaps: Enclosed space permit did not include a CO2 check, and no CO2-capable meter was supplied.
Safety officer checklist findings had no target date or actual close-out date.
Breath alcohol tester was past the maker's calibration interval (6 to 12 months or 200 tests).
condition: Intrinsically safe light outside the pumproom badly corroded.
Bunker line valves outside the pumproom not marked with the tanks they serve.
Main steam line valve from the engine room leaking; rust weeping from all mooring winch save-alls.
Forward liferaft painter secured to the cradle.
Purifier room manhole not highlighted as a trip hazard.
Generator top bolt covers cracked or missing; a cargo pump overspeed trip button not labelled.
ECDIS mouse and keyboard not on the maker's approved hardware list.
crew: Officers and crew performed satisfactorily.
stories.headline: Deck first, papers last: a practical Rotterdam inspection
stories.dek: A practical inspector walked the deck, pumproom and CCR before the paperwork; he kept every recorded finding but agreed to adjust its wording.
takeaways: If you disagree with an observation, ask for clearer wording rather than deletion.
Track the alcohol tester's calibration by both date and number of tests.
Check liferaft painters are attached through the weak link as designed, not tied to the cradle.

stories.style: Rated tough. Very senior, with decades of inspecting. Set clear rules at the opening meeting: anything recorded stays, even if closed out. Courteous, gave time to find evidence, relaxed with ratings, and expected short, direct answers.

negatives.text: Annual, intermediate and class attendance survey reports had not been filed in the enhanced survey file for years; they were printed and filed afterwards.
The HVPQ was out of date: the last PSC, last ballast tank inspection and last winch brake test entries had not been updated.
Free-fall lifeboat drills were logged as manoeuvring ahead and astern without releasing the falls, contrary to the guidelines.
Senior deck officer did not know the company procedure for free-fall or simulated launching of the lifeboat.
One portable multi-gas meter had been landed ashore for maintenance; a defect report had been raised.
The second multi-gas meter read 3.5 ppm H2S on 25 ppm test gas and its CO display was blank; sensors were renewed before completion.
Flame screens on vent pipes of the block-and-bleed valve system were damaged, and no maintenance task existed for them.
The fresh water generator ejector suction line had a temporary weld build-up repair, with no defect raised.
The engine team had not raised a defect for the temporary repair on the seawater line.
HVPQ photo 15 was meant to show the starboard manifold but showed the port manifold.
HVPQ photo 16 also showed the port manifold instead of the starboard one.

questions.q: Show the enhanced survey (ESP) file and explain what it contains.
Show the audits declared in the PIQ, including the Master's navigation audit.
How do you report a near miss or hazardous occurrence?
Show behaviour-based safety training certificates and records.
Compare work and rest hour records against the bell book.
Explain damage stability and the ship-specific actions if a compartment floods.
What is the company procedure for ECDIS alarm filtering, and which layers may be switched off?
Show how the radars are interswitched, as declared in the HVPQ.
Show BNWAS and Aldis lamp test records and the PMS job for the whistle.
Show the annual ECDIS performance test record.
Walk through the restricted visibility checklist and the bridge manning policy.
What voluntary security reporting scheme applies to this passage?
On the deck round, explain rescue boat and freefall lifeboat checks.
Start the emergency generator and explain the checks.
Are spool pieces and reducers marked with their pressure test details?
How is the double hull space inerted?
What are the retirement criteria for mooring ropes in the line management plan?
Show ballast tank inspection and safety officer inspection records.
Show gas meter test and calibration records.
What is the procedure for sampling toxic cargo?
Demonstrate donning and checking an SCBA.
Show PMS jobs and the critical spares list.
Explain the hot work procedure.
Where are the engineers' immersion suits, and when was the emergency generator last tested?

gaps: Enclosed space permit guidance notes did not match the SMS procedure, leaving users unsure which to follow.
Main engine failure drill was missing from the drill plan.
Security risk assessment not included in the passage plan.
Latest COSWP edition not on board, awaiting supply.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: annual ECDIS performance test was over a year overdue.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: an old UKC policy was still posted on the bridge next to the current one.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: monthly gas meter calibration was poorly logged.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: HVPQ listed a PV valve for double hull inerting that the ship did not have.
condition: Forward starboard winch and windlass hydraulic block leaking oil.
One foam monitor valve leaking; spare on order.
One portable gas meter damaged and on a deferred defect awaiting supply.
Tank domes corroded; manholes, sighting ports and forward steam branch lines needed maintenance.
crew: Senior deck officer did not know the free-fall launch procedure
Earlier deck and engine teams left gaps in survey records, drills and defect reporting
Deck officers and crew performed below average; engineer officers did well.
Weak SMS knowledge and filing led to slow answers, a longer inspection and an irritated inspector.
Flagged by inspector: a crew member could not show how to switch on the rescue boat searchlight.
Flagged by inspector: an officer was unsure of the voluntary security reporting scheme.
stories.headline: Eleven observations: lifeboat drills, gas meters and HVPQ errors
stories.dek: A heavy result: free-fall lifeboat drills done wrongly, both gas meters out of action, an outdated HVPQ with wrong photos and unrecorded temporary repairs.
takeaways: Update the HVPQ after every PSC, tank inspection and brake test, and check each photo shows what its caption says.
Know what your free-fall drill procedure requires and log exactly what was done.
Keep enough calibrated gas meters on board; losing one to shore repair can leave you short.
Fix defects before the inspector finds them; once recorded, even a closed-out item stays in the report.
Remove superseded posters, like an old UKC policy, from the bridge.

negatives.text: No written process for maintaining certificates on board; the electronic upload was not described in the SMS and only the office tracked expiry dates.
A public toilet near the CCR was out of order pending spare parts.
The toilet failure had not been entered in the defect reporting system.
Neither the policy manual nor the PMS reflected the maker's two-yearly ECDIS hard drive replacement, and no replacement was recorded.
Junior deck officer did not know the maker's requirement to replace the ECDIS hard drive every two years.
A free-fall lifeboat launch and in-water manoeuvre was logged, but crew interviews showed nobody boarded and the boat was never released; the Master and C/O of that time had left.
Senior deck officer had not noticed that the recovery motor was left fitted on the aft emergency towing-off wire winch, against the maker's requirements.

crew: Junior deck officer was unaware of the ECDIS hard drive replacement interval
Senior engineer let a failure go unreported in the defect system
Drill records did not match what the crew said had happened
stories.headline: A lifeboat drill on paper that never happened
stories.dek: Seven observations, led by a logged free-fall lifeboat launch that crew said never took place, plus ECDIS maintenance and defect reporting gaps.
takeaways: Never record a drill that was not done as written; inspectors interview the crew named in the record.
Know the maker's ECDIS maintenance items, such as hard drive replacement, and check they are in the PMS.
Enter every defect, even a broken toilet, in the defect reporting system.

negatives.text: The permanent means of access manual had no inspection or maintenance records for platforms, ladders or rails in any cargo or ballast tank (SOLAS II-1/3-6).
Enclosed space entry procedures had not been revised for the enhanced CO2 monitoring required by IMO MSC.581(110).

positives.text: Knew the passage plan appraisal form well, including the required assessments and documentation standards.
Explained emergency generator start precautions and started it successfully on both primary and secondary starters.

crew: Junior deck officers performed well on passage planning and the emergency generator
stories.headline: Empty access manual records and an outdated entry procedure
stories.dek: Two observations, a blank permanent means of access record and entry procedures missing the new CO2 checks, offset by two junior officer positives.
takeaways: Fill in the permanent means of access manual records after every tank inspection; blank pages become an observation.
Confirm your enclosed space procedure includes CO2 monitoring under MSC.581(110).
Practise emergency generator starts on both the primary and secondary means.

stories.style: Initial Paris MoU inspection by two PSCOs covering bridge and GMDSS, CCR and pump room, engine room, steering gear, decks and galley, with live tests of alarms, pumps and the emergency generator.
stories.headline: Initial PSC inspection, no deficiencies after a long test list
stories.dek: A Paris MoU initial inspection that tested engine room alarms, fire pumps, the emergency generator and cargo overfill alarms, and ended with no deficiencies.
takeaways: Expect live tests of engine room alarms: oil mist detector, fuel leak, bilge, generator low lube oil pressure and fire detection.
Have the 15 ppm OWS ready to demonstrate, along with quick-closing valves and the incinerator water mist.
Be ready to run the main and emergency fire pumps with three hoses forward and aft.

stories.style: Rated tough. Young and thorough; dug deep into documents and the SMS software, pressed for quick evidence, spotted cover-ups and said so. Focused on deck safety and procedural compliance; considerate in crew interviews but quick to record.

negatives.text: Junior deck officer could not explain how X-band and S-band radars differ in performance, or in which conditions S-band works better.
Senior deck officer did not know the MOB and recovery-from-water drill procedure; drill records showed no check of wind, sea and swell as the recovery plan requires.
Senior deck officer did not know the working-at-height procedure and admitted the required risk assessment had not been done before the job.
Senior deck officer did not know the company minimum stock of toxic gas detector tubes; mercaptan tubes had been missed in the last inventory.
Fire hoses on the deck foam and fire main lines were in poor condition, with corroded seizing.
The senior deck officer's last monthly safety inspection had not captured the condition of the foam and fire hoses.

positives.text: Knew his man overboard muster duty and talked through real MOB scenarios, from raising the general alarm to releasing the lifebuoy.
Explained safe rigging and recovery of the portable gangway and its parts, including the safety net and inclinometer.

gaps: SMS did not set a review frequency for risk assessments of routine jobs.
Final CAP certificate, latest IAMSAR and the C/O's BTM certificate not on board; BBS training incomplete.
Emergency checklists were not completed during drills.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: passage plan amended during pilotage was not updated in ECDIS for monitoring.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: time of monthly alcohol test not recorded; rest hours inconsistent for the last bunkering.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: navigational warnings missing for the period the ship was in dry dock abroad.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: engine room unmanning not logged on the bridge; MOB drill not logged in the engine log.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: recovery-from-water drill did not reference SOLAS or company guidance.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: office close-out comments on defects simply repeated the defect description.
condition: Steam lines painted over existing rust rather than properly treated.
Freefall lifeboat pick-up hook had no SWL marked and its safety latch spring did not work.
Spanners missing from fire hose boxes; foam monitor valve handle locks not working.
BWTS flowmeter and fixed gas detection alarms active during inspection; BWTS could not be run.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: an ullage port cap left open on a cargo tank.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: four inert gas valves not chained and padlocked.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: drums unsecured in the forecastle store; damaged fire hoses not marked condemned.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: rough anti-skid paint on warping drums that would damage natural-fibre ropes.
crew: Senior deck officer drew four Human observations on drills, work at height, gas tubes and safety rounds
Junior deck officer could not compare X-band and S-band radar performance
Ratings answered MOB and gangway questions confidently
2/O did not answer basic questions to SIRE 2.0 standard.
Inspector judged the C/O's answers inadequate, though the consultant found them acceptable.
Flagged by inspector: an officer was unaware of the electrostatic hazard linked to radar use.
stories.headline: Ratings shine, senior deck officer collects four Human observations
stories.dek: Six observations, mostly on senior deck officer knowledge of drills, work at height and gas detection, balanced by two strong rating interviews.
takeaways: Record wind, sea state and swell in MOB and recovery drill records, as your recovery-from-water plan requires.
Know the company minimum stock of gas detector tubes for each type and check it at every inventory.
Complete the risk assessment before any work at height starts, every time.
Clear active alarms (BWTS, gas detection) and secure stores before a planned inspection.
Never try to cover up a finding; inspectors notice, and it hardens their approach.

negatives.text: Enclosed space procedures did not address extra precautions, such as chlorine checks, for ballast tanks treated by an electrolysis BWMS; crew relied on the maker's statement.
During a routine pumproom safety inspection the officer missed two safety chains left unconnected at open vertical ladder accesses.
Company bunkering procedures did not require checks of bunker tank ullage space atmosphere for flammable vapour before, during or after bunkering.

positives.text: Junior deck officer clearly explained the different performance and uses of X-band and S-band radars.

stories.headline: Three findings and a radar compliment in a Shell inspection
stories.dek: Two procedure gaps and one missed safety chain, balanced by a positive for a junior officer who knew exactly when to use X-band and S-band radar.
takeaways: If your BWMS uses electrolysis, check the enclosed space procedure covers chlorine and by-product risks.
Make sure bunkering procedures require flammable vapour checks in bunker tank ullage spaces.
On pumproom rounds, check every safety chain at ladder openings is connected.

gaps: Restricted visibility checklist said steering in auto, contradicting the requirement for manual steering.
Master's standing orders did not set out lines of authority.
GMDSS log mixed up weekly and monthly tests; some EGC message types were not selected.
Passage plan kept identical arrival and departure drafts for a 13-day passage and wrongly flagged a PSSA.
Magnetron running hours did not match installation dates; barometer had no calibration certificate.
COSWP on board was the previous edition, and some security-related charts had expired.
Helicopter operations guide available only as a soft copy.
No equipment inventory in the SMPEP spill locker.
condition: Cargo pump trip interlock with N2 pressure bypassed by a wire jumper; pumps did not trip when line pressure fell.
Lifeboat door seal cut, so the door was no longer watertight.
Rescue boat engine kill-cord missing and starting instructions not posted at the engine.
Pilot ladder secured to a gangway airline instead of pad eyes; the pad eyes had no SWL marked.
Engine room blower coamings thinned, corroded and pinholed.
Cable and pipe openings into the hydraulic room not sealed with fire-retardant material.
Steering gear tank gauge glass cracked; telephone buttons in the steering room damaged.
Liferaft securing straps frayed; embarkation ladder pad eyes corroded.
crew: 3/O could not present their own areas; the 2/O and a junior officer showed items instead.
Three cadets interviewed were progressing well with their training.
Master stayed calm throughout; other officers and engineers were satisfactory.
stories.headline: A Coast Guard visit and a bypassed cargo pump trip
stories.dek: During a USCG compliance exam, the attending consultant's walk-round found a wired-out cargo pump interlock, a cut lifeboat door seal and many bridge record slips.
takeaways: Never bypass safety interlocks; prove cargo pumps trip on low N2 or deck line pressure.
Check lifeboat door seals, rescue boat kill-cords and liferaft straps before any port state visit.
Secure the pilot ladder to SWL-marked strong points, never to pipework.

stories.style: Rated normal. Senior, courteous and soft-spoken; spent most time interviewing crew, enclosed space entry his favourite topic. Listened for key words, prompted when stuck, rarely went deep into documents, and cut findings himself but would not negotiate at closing.

negatives.text: An anchor had recently been lost; it was reported to class and recorded in the defect system, with the replacement awaited.
The safety construction certificate was only conditionally valid for a short period because of the missing anchor.
Earth cables to the bridge wing searchlights were broken; they were repaired during the inspection.
One emergency light on the main deck was not working.
Brake drums on the aft starboard mooring winches were heavily rusted and uneven.

positives.text: Explained ECDIS set-up in detail: alarms and warnings, safety parameters, look-ahead and route checking.
Explained the galley portable extinguisher, fixed CO2 system and fire blanket.
Explained entry in detail: permission, RA, PPE, communication, emergency plans, ventilation, gas testing, standby person and permit.
Explained the entry procedure and his role in signing the permit as attendant or entrant.
Explained periodic checks on specialist working-at-height and over-side PPE and equipment.
Explained the company safe working procedure for work over the side.
Explained safe rigging and recovery of the pilot boarding arrangements and the precautions involved.
Explained and demonstrated manual emergency generator starting by battery and hydraulic means.

gaps: Familiarisation checklist had no section for galley crew.
SMS set a 1-hour gap between chart updates on the two ECDIS, but the familiarisation checklist said one day.
An anchor had been lost; a deferred defect and class condition were still open.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: brake drums rusting on several mooring winches.
Port rules limited the deck round to the inspector, the 3/O and one AB.
condition: Cargo tank dome leaking, manifold valves not holding and several manifold drain lines leaking.
Hard rust along fire, fresh water and air lines; several small pipe supports wasted.
Fresh water line flanges corroded and leaking on deck.
Remaining anchor thinned near the swivel collar.
Bow thruster out of use; a ballast tank level sensor and a store supply fan not working.
440 V insulation monitor alarm set at 2 megohms, judged not in line with SIRE expectations.
Tank gauging system in alarm during the inspection.
crew: Junior deck officers and ratings earned eight positives between them
No Human negatives: all five observations were equipment or certificate issues
Crew handled interview questions well; interview preparation was evident.
stories.headline: Eight crew positives, but a lost anchor and rusty winch brakes
stories.dek: Five observations tied to equipment, including a lost anchor and its conditional certificate, against eight positives for well-prepared officers and ratings.
takeaways: If equipment is lost, show the class report, defect entry and replacement plan straight away.
Check earth cables and emergency lights on deck rounds; small electrical faults still become observations.
Inspect mooring winch brake drums for rust and wear, not just the brake test records.
Practise enclosed space entry answers until every crew member can explain them in clear, precise terms.
Speak slowly and clearly; some inspectors listen for specific key words.

stories.style: Rated easy-going. Structured and considerate; explained the plan at the opening meeting and offered to adjust it around operations. Stuck strictly to the tablet with little cross-questioning, checked that records existed rather than their depth.
gaps: Safety inspection checklist had no ship-specific list of hot surfaces.
SMS unclear on how far from the planned route navigational warnings must be plotted.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: drill planner lacked emergency towing, hazardous cargo reaction and critical machinery failure drills.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: extended class survey status not uploaded to the OCIMF site.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: a diversion to anchorage was not added to the passage plan.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: manifold Y-pieces and U-bends not stencilled.
condition: One gangway roller wheel worn by about 40%.
Several ballast tank gauge floats, including a high level float, not working.
Pilot ladder securing pad eyes not marked with SWL.
Flagged by inspector, not recorded: fire door from the accommodation to the bridge not closing properly.
Engine room emergency escape has a mid-platform that would hinder evacuating a casualty.
Winch brake tightening marks faded away.
crew: 2/O struggled to show procedures or explain the anchorage diversion, EGC setup and BNWAS records.
C/O could not show anemometer or secondary venting alarm settings and confused bump tests with span gas stock.
C/O became argumentative with the inspector.
stories.headline: An easy inspector, but officers who couldn't show their work
stories.dek: A calm, by-the-tablet inspector spent two hours with the Master; the weak spots were officers who could not demonstrate their own records and settings.
takeaways: Know your own equipment settings: anemometer alarms, secondary venting alarms, EGC message types.
Record any diversion, such as to an anchorage, as a passage plan amendment.
Don't argue with the inspector; explain calmly and show evidence.

negatives.text: The certificate file index required by the SMS was missing from both statutory certificate files.
A crankcase inspection with web deflection was logged in the PMS, but no enclosed space entry permit had been completed for it.
A ballast water treatment filter in the pump room was leaking water continuously.
The same filter's differential pressure transmitter display was blank, while the CCR indicators showed 0.05 bar.
The SMS required an OWS operational check within 24 hours before arrival, logged in the engine log and oil record book; none was recorded for this port.

crew: Senior deck officer could not produce the certificate file index
Senior engineer had not done the pre-arrival OWS check
stories.headline: A crankcase entry without a permit and a missed OWS check
stories.dek: Five observations: a crankcase entered without an enclosed space permit, a missing pre-arrival OWS test, a leaking BWTS filter and a certificate index gap.
takeaways: Treat crankcase inspections as enclosed space entries and raise the permit every time.
Do the pre-arrival OWS test your SMS requires and log it in both the engine log and oil record book.
Keep the certificate file index current in every certificate folder.

negatives.text: Junior deck officer had not highlighted where the route crossed the safety contour on the passage plan.
Two explosion-proof deck lights had loose securing caps with exposed threads, and at least three more had been painted over, compromising their flame paths.
Monthly safety inspections had not picked up the defective gas-tight light fittings.

positives.text: Knew the galley firefighting arrangements well, including correct use of the CO2 extinguisher.

crew: Junior deck officer missed marking a safety contour crossing
Rating did well on galley firefighting
stories.headline: Painted-over flameproof lights and an unmarked safety contour
stories.dek: Three observations, a passage plan missing a safety contour crossing and flameproof deck lights left unsafe, with one positive for a rating.
takeaways: Mark every safety contour crossing on the passage plan and the ECDIS route.
Never paint over explosion-proof light fittings; paint ruins the flame path.
Check securing caps on flameproof fittings near the pump room and battery locker during rounds.

negatives.text: The oil spill pump on the aft deck was not working.
On one cargo tank the high-level alarm and level gauge disagreed: the alarm showed high level while the gauge read about 87%.
The senior deck officer's safety inspection had missed the defective oil spill pump; it was fixed during the inspection.
The senior deck officer had not noticed the mismatched tank level indication during cargo operations; it was fixed during the inspection.

positives.text: Explained the performance differences between X-band and S-band radars.
Explained entry procedures: permission, gas testing, RA, PPE, communication, emergency equipment, permit and continuous monitoring.
Explained the entry procedure and his role in signing the permit as attendant or entrant.
Explained manual emergency generator starting by battery and spring starter.

crew: Junior deck officers earned three positives
Senior deck officer missed a failed spill pump and a tank level mismatch
stories.headline: Juniors score positives, deck round misses two defects
stories.dek: Four observations around a broken oil spill pump and a tank alarm that disagreed with its gauge, against four positives for junior officers and a rating.
takeaways: Test the deck oil spill pump during safety rounds and before every cargo operation.
Compare tank gauge readings with high-level alarm status during cargo work and question any mismatch.
Junior officers: be ready to start the emergency generator by every means fitted.

negatives.text: A fire incident days before the inspection was not in the PIQ because the PIQ had already been submitted; reporting and investigation were otherwise correct.
The mechanical seal on the vacuum condenser cooling seawater pump was leaking; it was entered in the defect list once pointed out.
About 3% of the cargo heating pipework showed corrosion; repairs were under way with only the midships section left.

positives.text: Confidently explained starting the emergency fire pump manually, step by step, including the different starting locations.
Explained over-side work requirements: lifejacket, harness, fall arrester, work planning meeting, permit and risk assessment.

crew: Ratings earned positives on the emergency fire pump and over-side work
stories.headline: A recent fire missing from the PIQ, and praise for two ratings
stories.dek: Three observations, a PIQ overtaken by a recent incident and two hardware defects, against two positives for confident ratings.
takeaways: If an incident happens after the PIQ is submitted, update the PIQ or tell the inspector at the opening meeting.
Record leaks in the defect list before the inspector finds them.
Ratings should know every location from which the emergency fire pump can be started.

negatives.text: During sampling of a toxic and flammable cargo, the rating did not wear the face shield and gas-tight suit with breathing apparatus required by company procedure.

positives.text: Explained ECDIS set-up in detail: alarms and warnings, safety parameters, route checking and look-ahead.
Explained the performance differences between X-band and S-band radars and the ARPA units fitted.
Explained how to operate the wheeled fire extinguisher near the boiler.
Covered entry from permission, gas testing and RA to ventilation, standby person, toolbox meeting and continuous monitoring.
Explained manual emergency generator starting by battery and hydraulic means.

crew: Junior deck officers earned four positives across ECDIS, radar, entry and the emergency generator
A rating skipped the required face shield and gas-tight suit during cargo sampling
stories.headline: Five positives, one rating caught without full PPE at sampling
stories.dek: A single Human observation for missing PPE during toxic cargo sampling, against five positives for officers and ratings on navigation and safety.
takeaways: Wear the full PPE your procedure requires for toxic cargo sampling: face shield, gas-tight suit and breathing apparatus.
Junior officers: rehearse ECDIS safety settings, look-ahead and route checks out loud.
Be ready to compare X-band and S-band radar performance; inspectors keep asking.

negatives.text: The HVPQ contained errors in its mooring section (item 10.1.4).
Ship security drills must be held at least every three months, but the gap between drills had stretched to four months.
Calibration of the portable gas measuring instruments had expired about two months before the inspection.
The pressure and temperature calibrators used to cross-check the fixed tank gauging were out of calibration, certificates expired for two months.

stories.headline: Expired calibrations and a security drill that ran late
stories.dek: Four process and hardware observations: an HVPQ error, a security drill interval overrun and two sets of instruments past their calibration dates.
takeaways: Track calibration due dates for gas meters and gauging calibrators in the PMS and send them ashore well before expiry.
Count the days between ship security drills; three months is the maximum interval, not a target.
Cross-check the HVPQ against the latest records, especially mooring equipment entries, before every inspection.

negatives.text: The ECDIS familiarisation checklist did not refer to the Nautical Institute industry recommendations for ECDIS familiarisation, and that publication was not on board.
No certificate was available for the spare magnetic compass.

stories.headline: Montreal: two paperwork findings on the bridge
stories.dek: Both observations were process gaps: an ECDIS familiarisation checklist missing its industry reference, and no certificate for the spare magnetic compass.
takeaways: Base the ECDIS familiarisation checklist on the Nautical Institute industry recommendations and carry the publication.
Keep certificates for spare equipment, including the spare magnetic compass.
Spares are inspected too: their documents matter as much as those of the fitted equipment.

negatives.text: Two of four brackets for the removable guard rail stanchions around the engine room stores hatch were wasted and unusable.
The area safety inspection done earlier that month had recorded the same guard rails as in place, secure and in good condition.
SMS gave no description of the SSO's role or duties beyond a catch-all clause; SSO said duties were only in the confidential SSP. Some records lacked SSO signatures.
Rating on cargo watch was nervous and could not explain precautions for ullaging or sampling static accumulator cargo in non-inerted tanks, saying it was not his duty.
Mooring system management plan did not state the minimum number of lines per service needed to meet design limits at a standard jetty or buoy mooring.

positives.text: Senior deck officer explained portable gas meter testing requirements in detail and knew the specific instruments on board in depth.
Rating explained the steps and precautions for rigging the shore gangway in detail; the inspector also saw it done while waiting to board.

stories.headline: Beaumont: a record that said the guard rails were fine
stories.dek: Five negatives and two positives: wasted guard rail brackets signed off as good, a vague SSO role, a nervous cargo watch rating and a gap in the mooring plan.
takeaways: Area safety inspections must reflect real condition; inspectors compare the record with what they see.
Every rating on cargo watch must know static accumulator precautions, whatever their usual duties.
Define the SSO's duties in the SMS, not only in the confidential SSP.

negatives.text: No company procedure required the coating technical file to be kept to class guidance; the SMS only recommended filing one.
A cargo audit finding on isolating fixed gas detection at sea was closed within two days as 'all crew trained', but no training record backed it up.
ECDIS offered standard, base and custom display modes, but company procedures gave no clear guidance on display management.
A guard rail on an upper pump room platform next to the emergency escape was bent by about 45 degrees and had not been picked up.
The personnel transfer basket had no record of the proof and two-yearly load tests required by company policy; it was tagged out of use.
No company procedure covered operation, testing and maintenance of inert gas plant parts such as the boiler uptake valves and gas regulating valve.

crew: Junior deck officer could not show load test records for the personnel transfer basket
stories.headline: Six observations, four of them gaps in company procedures
stories.dek: Process findings dominated: missing procedures for coatings, ECDIS display and inert gas plant, an audit closed without proof and an untested transfer basket.
takeaways: When closing an audit finding, file the evidence such as training records the same day.
Check the personnel transfer basket certificate and load test dates before any crane transfer.
Know which ECDIS display mode your company expects and why; ask the office if the SMS is silent.

negatives.text: A hydraulic line connection on an aft mooring winch was corroded.
The main deck steam line and manifold showed significant corrosion in several places.
The main cargo line forward of the accommodation had scattered rust spots.
Insulating rubber mats were missing at the 450V transformers in the emergency generator room; mats were laid once pointed out.
The senior deck officer's deck safety inspection about a month earlier had not recorded any of these defects.
A generator engine fuel oil quick-closing valve did not work because of a defective air cylinder; the cylinder was renewed during the inspection.
The machinery space safety inspection a month earlier had not picked up the defective quick-closing valve.
No company procedure covered inspection and testing of vapour and inert gas pipelines.
The emergency generator quick-closing valve was not included in its monthly maintenance routine.

positives.text: Knew the enclosed space entry procedure well, including the attendant's duties and the gas checks needed before entry.

crew: Junior deck officer was well versed in enclosed space entry
Senior deck officer and senior engineer safety rounds missed visible defects
stories.headline: Rust, missing mats and safety rounds that saw nothing
stories.dek: Nine observations, mostly deck and engine room defects that recent monthly safety inspections had failed to record, plus two procedure gaps.
takeaways: Treat monthly safety rounds as a hunt: record corrosion, missing mats and failed valves before the inspector does.
Test quick-closing valves, including the emergency generator's, and make sure they are in the PMS.
Check rubber insulating mats are in place at all switchboards and transformers.

negatives.text: The class status report showed two open items with due dates: a temporary repair on a fuel oil tank sounding pipe and leaks on two cargo condensers.
The dynamic navigational audit declared in the PIQ had been carried out with the vessel at anchor, not on passage.
No electrical power failure drill had been held since the change of operator some months earlier, although company procedures required one.
Ventilation flaps for the cargo motor room fans were seized in the open position.
The senior deck officer had not maintained the motor room fan vent flaps.

crew: Senior deck officer was held responsible for a missed blackout drill and unmaintained vent flaps
stories.headline: After a change of operator, drills and vent flaps fell behind
stories.dek: Five observations, from open class items and a navigational audit done at anchor to a missed blackout drill and seized motor room vent flaps.
takeaways: After a change of operator, run every drill the new SMS requires; old drill records may not count.
Navigational audits must be done on passage; one carried out at anchor will be challenged.
Exercise ventilation flaps and closures regularly so they close when needed.

stories.style: Gave a time plan per area at the opening meeting and expected about 9 hours. Wanted answers only from the person asked; seniors and the superintendent were told not to intervene. Hands-on: had lifeboats run, emergency generator started and alarms tested.

questions.q: Show PMS records and explain the company defect reporting procedure.
Start the lifeboat engine and show ahead, astern and rudder movement.
Show the lifeboat food rations, first aid kit and pyrotechnics.
Switch on all deck lights, including the emergency lighting.
Operate and reset the emergency generator fuel quick-closing valve, then start the generator on battery.
Demonstrate donning an immersion suit and the checks you make before putting it on.
Explain the enclosed space entry procedure.
Describe every step of rigging a pilot ladder, from start to finish.
Where is the fire pump started, and how are the quick-closing valves and fire flaps operated?
Show the PMS record for maintenance of gas welding flashback arrestors.
What engine room watch level applies now, and what does the company procedure say?
Who is in charge of safety in the engine room?
When was the last blackout drill, and what is the company procedure?
How often are the emergency generator load test, emergency steering and local manoeuvring tested, and when last?
Show the fuel transfer procedure, its records and the lube oil analysis frequency.
What do you do in a hot plate fire, and how is the galley fixed CO2 system activated?
What is the company procedure for working aloft?
Show cargo pump purging records.
Explain the company procedures for inerting and gas freeing.
Show maintenance records for chemical protective suits.
Show the procedure and records for PV valve overhaul, N2 isolation and double block and bleed valves.
Show gas meter calibration records and the company procedure.
Show safety familiarisation records for shore personnel who boarded.
What special precautions apply to inhibited cargo?
Walk through the discharge plan and the company loading and discharging procedures.
Is the pilot part of the bridge team, and where is that recorded?
What is the UKC policy at berth, at buoy moorings, in transit and in open sea?
Which ECDIS safety parameters does the SMS require?
How do you tell coastal from open waters, and where does the SMS define it?
Where does the SMS set CPA and TCPA limits for coastal and open waters?
How do you decide visibility is restricted?
Does the company have a distraction policy on the bridge?
How do you test the echo sounder shallow-depth alarm, when was it last done and where is it logged?
Show the procedure and records for checking the Aldis lamp, sound signals and navigation lights.
How often is the autopilot heading checked against the magnetic compass?
How do you decide the bridge watch level, and where is it recorded?
Explain how you use radar guard zones and the trial manoeuvre.
Show UKC calculations for each leg and the position-fixing intervals in the passage plan.

stories.headline: Shell in Boston: nine and a half hours, answers from the person asked
stories.dek: Boarding mid-afternoon and leaving near midnight, the inspector toured every space, ran lifeboats and alarms, and questioned each rank directly with no prompting allowed.
takeaways: Expect to answer alone: seniors and the superintendent may be told to stay silent.
Be ready to run lifeboats ahead and astern, start the emergency generator on battery and reset quick-closing valves.
2/O: know UKC policy per stage, ECDIS safety settings, CPA/TCPA limits and where the SMS defines each.

11.style: Rated normal. Calm, smiling and direct; explained his plan and kept everyone busy. Mostly followed the tablet with some cross-questioning, showed extra interest in the engine room and spent about 20 minutes probing drill records and real understanding.

negatives.text: A generator engine lube oil low-pressure trip failed when tested on request, due to a faulty pressure regulating valve; fixed before departure. Class had tested it days earlier.
Senior engineer was not fully familiar with the local function test of the oil mist detector using its optical test pieces; the requested test was not seen.

positives.text: Very familiar with enclosed space entry: formal authorisation, signed permit, isolation of energy sources and thorough atmosphere testing.
Knew the safety meeting agenda in full: old business, incidents and near misses, equipment status, crew feedback and operations review.

gaps: Safety depth calculation left out CATZOC and tide, unlike the UKC calculation, contrary to NP232 guidance.
No 'no distraction' policy posted in the CCR for cargo operations.
No written procedure for withdrawing gas detector tubes once new gas meters were supplied.
Drill planner did not specifically cover propulsion failure or emergency towing, as SIRE 2.0 expects.
Worst damaged stability case taken from standard conditions, not the actual loading condition.
Past tank cleaning not recorded in the CCR log; ODME clock 5 minutes off bridge UTC.
UKC poster on display was a different version from the one in the SMS.
Decommissioned decanting valve not marked as such and its hydraulic lines not blanked.
condition: Oil mist detector did not alarm when tested, and the test foil could not be found quickly.
A valve leaked after the low lube oil alarm test; a container was ready, showing a known leak.
Emergency fire pump discharge pressure did not rise after starting.
Gaps in pipe and cable runs into the hydraulic room left no fire protection.
Battery room exhaust fan not working.
Broken D-spanner in use; emergency fire pump pit handrail chain sagging, a fall hazard.
No shock treatment poster or rubber mats around the emergency generator room transformer.
Emergency steering control knob caps damaged and holed.
crew: Ratings impressed on enclosed space entry and safety meetings
Senior engineer struggled to demonstrate the oil mist detector test
Officers and engineers satisfactory; the 2/O and 3/O explained their areas well.
C/O struggled to show procedures.
ETO could not trigger the insulation monitor alarm in a reasonable time.
11.headline: Engine room trip fails under test, ratings earn two positives
11.dek: Two engine room observations, a failed lube oil trip test and an unclear oil mist detector check, against two positives for well-prepared ratings.
takeaways: Expect the inspector to ask for live trip tests on generators; test them yourself beforehand, not only at class surveys.
Engineers should be able to demonstrate the oil mist detector local test with its test pieces, step by step.
Brief ratings on the safety meeting agenda; inspectors ask them about it directly.
Test oil mist detector, insulation monitor and low lube oil alarms beforehand, with test kits to hand.
Include CATZOC and tide in the safety depth calculation, as in the UKC calculation.
